A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

derivations.claim: If $i$ and $j$ are adjacent, the one-edge path between them has no internal vertices, so it is active given every $S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ by [F1]. Hence no such $S$ d-separates them.

Suppose $i$ and $j$ are nonadjacent. Acyclicity implies that at least one of $i,j$ is not a descendant of the other; after interchanging labels, assume $j$ is not a descendant of $i$. Since $i,j$ are nonadjacent, $j$ is a non-descendant non-parent of $i$. Put $S=\operatorname{pa}_G(i)$. Then $S$ excludes both endpoints. Consider any path $i=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_r=j$. If its first arrow points into $i$, then $v_1\in S$ and the occurrence of $v_1$ is a noncollider, because the arrow $v_1\to i$ has its tail at $v_1$; the path is blocked. If the first arrow points out of $i$, follow arrows that point forward along the path until the first arrow that points backward. Such a reversal must occur because $j$ is not a descendant of $i$. At the reversal vertex $v_t$, both incident arrows point into $v_t$, so it is a collider and the initial segment is a directed path $i\to\cdots\to v_t$. If $v_t$ had a descendant $p\in S$, then $i\to\cdots\to v_t\to\cdots\to p\to i$ would be a directed cycle. Thus this collider has no descendant in $S$, and the path is blocked by [F1]. Every path is blocked, so $S$ d-separates $i$ and $j$.
The adjacent and nonadjacent cases prove both implications.

For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

derivations.claim: Put $P=\operatorname{pa}_G(x)$, so $\operatorname{pa}_G(y)=P\cup\{x\}$. If reversing the arrow created a directed cycle, that cycle would use the new arrow $y\to x$, and the remaining part would be a directed path $x\to\cdots\to z\to y$ in $G$ with $z\ne x$. Then $z\in P$, so $z\to x$ is also in $G$, making the directed cycle $x\to\cdots\to z\to x$ in $G$, a contradiction. Thus $G'$ is acyclic.

The full moral graphs of $G$ and $G'$ coincide. Their skeletons coincide. The only changed parent sets are $\operatorname{pa}_G(x)=P$, $\operatorname{pa}_G(y)=P\cup\{x\}$ and $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(x)=P\cup\{y\}$, $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)=P$. Any pair newly married at $y$ in $G$ or at $x$ in $G'$ already belongs to the clique on $P\cup\{x,y\}$: pairs involving $x$ or $y$ are skeleton edges, and pairs in $P$ are married at both $x$ and $y$. All other parent sets are unchanged, so the moral edge sets are identical.

Fix pairwise disjoint query sets $A,B,S$ and put $T=A\cup B\cup S$. The ancestor sets of $T$ in $G$ and $G'$ differ, if at all, only by $x$ or $y$. Indeed, a directed path whose existence changes must use the reversed edge. A path in $G$ that uses $x\to y$ and starts at $v\ne x$ enters $x$ from some $p\in P$; in $G'$ replace $p\to x\to y$ by the unchanged arrow $p\to y$. Therefore only $x$ can cease to be an ancestor. Symmetrically, a path in $G'$ using $y\to x$ and starting at $v\ne y$ enters $y$ from $p\in P=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)$; in $G$ replace $p\to y\to x$ by $p\to x$. Therefore only $y$ can become an ancestor. If $x$ is lost, $y$ belongs to both ancestor sets; if $y$ is gained, $x$ belongs to both.

If the ancestor sets are equal, step 1.2 shows the induced ancestral moral graphs are equal. Suppose instead that $x$ is an ancestor only in $G$. Then $x\notin T$ and $y$ is a common ancestor of $T$. In the moral graph induced on $\operatorname{An}_G(T)$, every neighbor of $x$ is in $P\cup\{y\}$: its parents lie in $P$; among its children only $y$ can be ancestral, since any other child has an unchanged arrow from $x$ and would make $x$ an ancestor in $G'$; and a marriage through a child other than $y$ would have the same consequence, while a marriage through $y$ uses another parent in $P$. The vertices in $P\cup\{y\}$ form a clique because they are parents of $y$ in $G$. Hence $x$ is simplicial in the ancestral moral graph. The case that $y$ is gained only in $G'$ is symmetric, with its neighbors contained in the clique $P\cup\{x\}$.

Removing an unconditioned simplicial vertex does not change separation between $A$ and $B$ after deleting $S$: the vertex is not in $T$, and any path through it can be shortened by replacing its two incident edges with the edge joining its neighbors, which exists because the neighborhood is a clique. Conversely, every path in the smaller graph remains in the larger graph. Thus the two ancestral moral graphs separate $A$ and $B$ by $S$ in exactly the same cases. By [F1], $G$ and $G'$ have the same d-separation relations.

derivations.claim: We first show by induction on the number of vertices that a connected noncomplete chordal graph has two nonadjacent simplicial vertices. Choose nonadjacent vertices $a,b$ and an inclusion-minimal separator $S$ whose removal disconnects them. Let $C_a,C_b$ be the components of $H-S$ containing $a,b$. For every $s\in S$, minimality gives a path from $a$ to $b$ after restoring only $s$, so $s$ has a neighbor in each of $C_a,C_b$. If $x,y\in S$ were nonadjacent, shortest paths from $x$ to $y$ with internal vertices in $C_a$ and in $C_b$ would form an induced cycle of length at least four: each path is chordless by shortestness, there are no edges between the two components, and $x,y$ are nonadjacent. This contradicts chordality, so $S$ is a clique. The induced graphs on $C_a\cup S$ and $C_b\cup S$ are smaller connected chordal graphs. By induction, each is either complete, in which case any vertex in its nonempty component $C_a$ or $C_b$ is simplicial, or noncomplete, in which case it has two nonadjacent simplicial vertices and at least one lies outside the clique $S$. Such a vertex has no neighbors outside its component together with $S$, so it is simplicial in $H$. The chosen vertices from $C_a$ and $C_b$ are nonadjacent. Complete connected graphs have every vertex simplicial, and disconnected graphs have a simplicial vertex in each component. Therefore every nonempty finite chordal graph has a simplicial vertex.

Repeatedly remove a simplicial vertex. Each induced subgraph remains chordal, so step 1.1 supplies a simplicial vertex until the graph is empty. The removal order $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a perfect elimination order because the neighbors of $v_t$ that remain at its removal are pairwise adjacent.

For each $t$, let $K_t=\{v_t\}\cup N_t^+$, where $N_t^+$ is the set of neighbors of $v_t$ later in the elimination order. Each $K_t$ is a clique by step 2.1. If $N_t^+$ is nonempty, let $p(t)$ be its earliest vertex and join the clique node $K_t$ to $K_{p(t)}$. The index strictly increases along parent edges, so these edges form a forest. Since $N_t^+$ is a clique, every vertex of $N_t^+$ other than $p(t)$ is a later neighbor of $p(t)$; hence $K_t\cap K_{p(t)}=N_t^+$. If a vertex $x$ belongs to $K_t$ with $t<x$, then $x\in N_t^+$ and this membership propagates to the parent node, eventually to $K_x$. Thus the clique nodes containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree. Every graph edge lies in some $K_t$ by taking its earlier endpoint. This is a clique forest with the running-intersection property.

Root one tree of this forest. Each vertex $x$ belongs to a connected subtree of clique nodes, so there is a unique root-nearest node $C_x$ containing it. Order the clique nodes in postorder, and list the vertices owned by each node $C_x$ in any order. For any neighbor $y$ of $x$, a clique node $D$ contains both. The nodes $C_x,C_y,D$ lie in the connected subtrees of cliques containing $x$ and $y$, so $C_x,C_y$ are comparable along the root-to-$D$ path. If $C_y$ is an ancestor of $C_x$, the running-intersection property gives $y\in C_x$; if it is a strict descendant of $C_x$, its block is earlier in postorder; and if it is $C_x$, both vertices are in the same clique block. Thus any neighbor $y$ later than $x$ belongs to the clique $C_x$. All later neighbors of $x$ therefore lie in the clique $C_x$, so this order is a perfect elimination order.

Direct every edge from its later endpoint in this order to its earlier endpoint. The orientation is acyclic because every arrow decreases the order. The parents of any vertex are among its later neighbors, which form a clique by step 4.1; hence there is no unshielded collider.

Since $\{u,v\}$ is an edge, some clique node $C$ contains both. Root its clique tree at $C$. Then $C$ is the root-nearest node containing each of $u,v$, so both are owned by its vertex block. List $v$ before $u$ in that block; step 5.1 directs $u\to v$. Reversing their order directs $v\to u$. The remaining vertices in the block may retain any order, and other trees may be rooted and ordered independently. Both resulting orientations are acyclic and collider-free by steps 4.1–5.1.

derivations.claim: First assume that $G_1,G_2$ have the same skeleton and the same unshielded colliders. A finite DAG has a topological order: if every remaining vertex had an incoming arrow, following incoming arrows in the finite graph would repeat a vertex and create a directed cycle; remove a source and repeat. Fix such an order $\prec$ for $G_1$. If the DAGs differ, choose the $\prec$-earliest vertex $\beta$ with $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_{G_2}(\beta)\ne\varnothing$, and choose the $\prec$-latest $\alpha$ in that difference. Then $\alpha\to\beta$ occurs in $G_1$ and $\beta\to\alpha$ in $G_2$.

Conversely, assume $G_1,G_2$ are Markov equivalent. If their skeletons differed, [F2] would give a pair separated in one graph but not the other. Thus their skeletons agree. If an unshielded collider $i\to k\leftarrow j$ occurred in $G_1$ but not in $G_2$, then $i,j$ are nonadjacent in both. By [F2] choose $S$ that d-separates $i,j$ in $G_1$. The path $i\to k\leftarrow j$ shows that no descendant of $k$, including $k$, can lie in $S$, because otherwise that path would be active. In $G_2$, the same unshielded triple has a noncollider at $k$; since $k\notin S$, the two-edge path is active, so $S$ does not d-separate $i,j$ there. This contradicts Markov equivalence. Interchanging $G_1,G_2$ rules out a collider present only in $G_2$.

Let $\gamma\ne\alpha$ be another parent of $\beta$ in $G_1$. If $\gamma$ were not a parent of $\alpha$, then either $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ would be nonadjacent, making $\alpha\to\beta\leftarrow\gamma$ an unshielded collider absent from $G_2$, or they would be adjacent with $\alpha\to\gamma$ in $G_1$. The first case contradicts equality of colliders; in the second case, $G_2$ cannot retain both $\alpha\to\gamma$ and $\gamma\to\beta$, because together with $\beta\to\alpha$ they form a directed cycle. If $\alpha\to\gamma$ is reversed in $G_2$, then $\gamma\prec\beta$ is an earlier vertex with a differing parent; if $\gamma\to\beta$ is reversed, then $\gamma$ is a later member than $\alpha$ of $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_{G_2}(\beta)$. Both contradict the choices in step 1.1. Hence every parent of $\beta$ other than $\alpha$ is a parent of $\alpha$.

To prove $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\alpha)\subseteq\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)$, suppose instead that $\gamma\to\alpha$ in $G_1$ but $\gamma\notin\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)$. Minimality of $\beta$ implies $\gamma\to\alpha$ is also present in $G_2$; otherwise the earlier vertex $\alpha$ would already have a differing parent. If $\gamma$ were not adjacent to $\beta$, then $G_2$ would contain the unshielded collider $\beta\to\alpha\leftarrow\gamma$, while $G_1$ has the noncollider chain $\gamma\to\alpha\to\beta$, contradicting equality of colliders. Thus $\gamma$ is adjacent to $\beta$. In $G_1$ it must be oriented $\gamma\to\beta$, since $\beta\to\gamma$ would make a directed cycle with $\gamma\to\alpha\to\beta$. This contradicts the assumption that $\gamma$ is not a parent of $\beta$. Therefore the inclusion holds. Together with step 2.1, $\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\beta)=\operatorname{pa}_{G_1}(\alpha)\cup\{\alpha\}$, so $\alpha\to\beta$ is covered.

Reverse this covered arrow in $G_1$. By [F3] the result remains a DAG and is Markov equivalent to $G_1$. It has the same skeleton, and it has the same unshielded colliders: an edge in an unshielded collider cannot be covered, because the other parent of the collider would then also be a parent of the edge's tail and hence adjacent to it. Exactly one edge now agrees with $G_2$, so the finite number of edge-orientation disagreements decreases by one. If any disagreement remains, choose the earliest differing parent set again; the argument in steps 1.1–3.1 applies because the skeleton and collider set are unchanged. Thus finitely many covered reversals transform $G_1$ into $G_2$, and each reversal preserves d-separation.
The two directions prove the equivalence.

For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of

distinct indices $i,j$ and $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, define
the conditional covariance block
$$
K_{ij\mid S}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}-\Sigma_{\{i,j\},S}\Sigma_{S,S}^{-1}\Sigma_{S,\{i,j\}},
$$
with $K_{ij\mid\varnothing}=\Sigma_{\{i,j\},\{i,j\}}$. Whenever the diagonal
entries of this block are positive, the **partial correlation** is
$$
\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{(K_{ij\mid S})_{12}}{\sqrt{(K_{ij\mid S})_{11}(K_{ij\mid S})_{22}}}.
$$
The nondegenerate Gaussian case makes the conditioning covariance block
invertible; the following theorem proves that $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive
definite, so this definition applies to every such $i,j,S$.

Let $x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)}\in\mathbb R^p$ be a sample, let $i\ne j$, and
let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i,j\}$. Let $\mathbf x_k\in\mathbb

projection onto the span of the all-ones vector and $\{\mathbf x_s:s\in S\}$.
When the sample covariance matrix of coordinates $\{i,j\}\cup S$ is positive
definite, define the residual columns
$$R_{i\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_i,\qquad R_{j\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_j.$$
The **sample partial correlation** is
$$\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{R_{i\mid S}^{T}R_{j\mid S}}{\|R_{i\mid S}\|_2\,\|R_{j\mid S}\|_2}.$$
For $-1<r<1$, the **Fisher transform** is
$g(r)=\frac12\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}$, and the sample Fisher statistic is
$Z_{ij\mid S}=g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})$. For a test using multiplier
$\sqrt{n-|S|-3}$, require $n-|S|-3>0$ so that this factor is positive. Under independent samples
from a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the stated covariance block is positive
definite almost surely whenever $n-|S|-3>0$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], each observation's pair $(X_i,X_j)$ is a linear function of $X_S$ plus a Gaussian residual independent of $X_S$ with covariance $K_{ij\mid S}$. Across observations these residual pairs are independent. The $S$ coordinates have a nondegenerate Gaussian density because their covariance is a positive-definite principal submatrix. If $|S|=0$, the intercept design has rank one. If $s=|S|>0$, successive independent sample points in $\mathbb R^s$ are affinely independent until there are $s+1$: after $r\le s$ affinely independent points, their affine span has dimension $r-1<s$, and the next point has a density, so lies in that span with probability zero by [F4]. Thus the intercept and $S$ design has rank $s+1$ almost surely. Conditional on that design, an orthonormal basis of its orthogonal complement has dimension $m=n-|S|-1$. In that basis the projected residual pairs are $m$ independent copies of this Gaussian residual; standardizing the two coordinates does not change their sample correlation. Thus the sample partial correlation has the same distribution as $R_m=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^m U_rV_r}{(\sum_{r=1}^mU_r^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{r=1}^mV_r^2)^{1/2}},\qquad m=n-|S|-1,$ for $m$ independent copies $(U_r,V_r)$ of the standardized pair, whose correlation is $\rho=\rho_{ij\mid S}$ by [F1]. The hypothesis gives $m\ge3$. Their covariance block is positive definite by [F3], so the first residual sample column is nonzero almost surely, and conditional on that column the second has a density in $\mathbb R^m$. Its probability of lying in the first column's one-dimensional span is zero by [F4], since $m\ge2$. Therefore $R_m\in(-1,1)$ almost surely and the Fisher transform is defined.

Represent $U_r=X_r$ and $V_r=\rho X_r+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}E_r$ with independent standard normal vectors $X,E\in\mathbb R^m$. Put $A=\|X\|$, $Z=\langle E,X/A\rangle$, and $W=\|E-ZX/A\|$. Rotational invariance of the standard Gaussian density implies that $A^2\sim\chi_m^2$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and $W^2\sim\chi^2_{m-1}$ are independent. Direct substitution gives $R_m=\frac{q}{\sqrt{q^2+W^2}},\qquad q=\frac{\rho A}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}+Z,$ and hence $g(R_m)=\operatorname{arsinh}(q/W)$. Rotational invariance follows directly from the standard Gaussian density, and it makes $A,Z,W$ independent. Also $\operatorname{arsinh}(\rho/\sqrt{1-\rho^2})=g(\rho)$.

Let $B=M/\sqrt{1-M^2}$ and $L=4B+2$. On the event $|A/\sqrt m-1|\le\delta,\quad |W/\sqrt m-1|\le\delta,\quad |Z|/\sqrt m\le\delta,$ where $0<\delta\le1/2$, one has $\left|\frac qW-\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right| \le \frac{(2B+1)\delta}{1-\delta}\le L\delta.$ Since $|\operatorname{arsinh}'(x)|=1/\sqrt{1+x^2}\le1$, step 2.1 yields $|g(R_m)-g(\rho)|\le L\delta$.

For $Q\sim\chi_k^2$, its moment generating function, obtained by multiplying the $k$ one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, is $\mathbb E e^{sQ}=(1-2s)^{-k/2}$ for $s<1/2$. For $\delta>0$, Markov's inequality optimized at $s=\delta/[2(1+\delta)]$ gives $\mathbb P(Q/k\ge1+\delta)\le e^{-k(\delta-\log(1+\delta))/2}$. For $0<\delta<1$, the negative choice $s=-\delta/[2(1-\delta)]$ gives $\mathbb P(Q/k\le1-\delta)\le e^{-k(-\delta-\log(1-\delta))/2}$. Put $\delta_+=2u+u^2\le3$ and $\delta_-=2u-u^2\ge u$. Set $\delta=t/L$. Since $L\ge2$ and $0<t\le1$, step 3.1 applies and its complement contains the event in the Statement. Step 4.1 therefore bounds that event by $6\exp(-mt^2/(64L^2))$. Taking $C_M=6$ and $c_M=(64L^2)^{-1}$ proves the claim.

Fix a finite vertex set $V$. For a DAG $G$ on $V$, its **skeleton** is the
undirected graph with edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $G$ contains $i\to j$ or
$j\to i$. An **unshielded triple** is a triple of distinct vertices $i,k,j$
with edges $i-k$ and $k-j$ in the skeleton and no edge between $i$ and $j$.
It is an **unshielded collider** (also called a v-structure) when its arrows are
$i\to k\leftarrow j$. Two DAGs on $V$ are **Markov equivalent** when they
induce the same d-separation relations: for every pairwise disjoint
$A,B,S\subseteq V$, $A$ and $B$ are d-separated by $S$ in one DAG exactly
when they are d-separated by $S$ in the other. The equivalence class of $G$ is
denoted $[G]$.

A **partially directed acyclic graph** (PDAG) on $V$ is a simple mixed graph
whose directed edges contain no directed cycle. A **consistent DAG extension**
of a PDAG preserves every directed edge, orients every undirected edge, is
acyclic, and creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. For an
equivalence class with a common skeleton, its **completed pattern** directs an
edge exactly when that orientation occurs in every DAG of the class and leaves
the edge undirected when both orientations occur. A **completed partially
directed acyclic graph** (CPDAG) for $[G]$ is this unique completed pattern
when its consistent DAG extensions are exactly $[G]$. Thus its directed edges
are compelled, while each undirected edge occurs in both directions among its
consistent extensions.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

**Output:** An undirected skeleton $C$, a separator record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$
for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.
Adjacency sets are read from the current graph, including deletions already
made at level $\ell$.

3. If at least one remaining edge has an endpoint with at least $\ell+1$
neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. For each unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, replace $i-k-j$ by
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$.

5. Repeatedly orient edges to closure under the following background-free rules,
using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Do not apply a background-knowledge rule.

Two finite DAGs on the same vertex set are Markov equivalent, meaning that they
induce the same d-separation relations, if and only if they have the same
skeleton and the same unshielded colliders.

An undirected graph is **chordal** when it has no induced cycle of length at
least four. A vertex is **simplicial** when all of its neighbors are pairwise
adjacent. A **perfect elimination order** is a total order in which the later
neighbors of each vertex form a clique. For every finite chordal undirected
graph $H$ and every edge $\{u,v\}$ of $H$, there are acyclic orientations of
all edges of $H$ with no unshielded collider $a\to w\leftarrow b$ with
$a,b$ nonadjacent, one having $u\to v$ and another having $v\to u$.

derivations.claim: Every consistent extension of a current pattern must respect each R1–R3 conclusion. For R1, the opposite orientation would create the new unshielded collider $i\to j\leftarrow k$ with $i,k$ nonadjacent. For R2, the opposite orientation would close the directed path $i\to k\to j$ into a directed cycle. For R3, if $j\to i$, acyclicity forces $k\to i$ and $\ell\to i$ (the alternatives $i\to k$ or $i\to\ell$ each close a directed cycle through $j$); these arrows create the new unshielded collider $k\to i\leftarrow\ell$, since $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent. Each contradiction is forbidden for a consistent extension. Thus all rule orientations are compelled, and the original DAG $G$ remains a consistent extension at every stage.

Every finite DAG has a topological order. In any nonempty induced subgraph, if every vertex had an incoming arrow, repeatedly following incoming arrows would revisit a vertex and create a directed cycle. Thus a source exists; remove one source and repeat on the remaining finite DAG. Listing the removed vertices in order gives a topological order, because an arrow's tail must be removed before its head. This argument uses only finite choices.

The R1–R3 closure reaches a final pattern after finitely many applications. Each scan checks finitely many rule instances on the finite vertex set; every nonterminal scan directs at least one previously undirected edge, and there are at most $\binom{|V|}{2}$ such edges. Therefore after finitely many scans a full scan applies no rule, so the final closed pattern $P$ used below exists.

Write $P$ for the final closed pattern. We claim that whenever $a\to b$ and $b-c$ is undirected in $P$, the edge $a-c$ is directed $a\to c$. If $a,c$ were nonadjacent, R1 would orient $b-c$ as $b\to c$, contradicting closure. If $c\to a$, then $c\to a\to b$ and R2 would orient $c-b$ as $c\to b$, also contradicting closure. It remains to rule out $a-c$ undirected.

Suppose such an undirected $a-c$ exists, and choose a counterexample for which the arrow $a\to b$ was first oriented as early as possible in the finite sequence of rule applications. If $a\to b$ was initially oriented as part of a collider $a\to b\leftarrow d$, then $a,d$ are nonadjacent. Since $d\to b-c$ cannot satisfy R1, $d$ is adjacent to $c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-b$ applies along $c\to d\to b$. If $d\to c$, R1 on $d\to c-a$ gives $c\to a$, and R2 on $c-b$ then applies along $c\to a\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, R3 on $c-b$ applies with its other two vertices $a,d$. Each case contradicts that $P$ is closed.

Iterating the claim in step 2.1 along an undirected path shows that a directed edge cannot have both endpoints in the same connected component of undirected edges: such a path from its head back to its tail would propagate $a\to b$ to a nonexistent loop $a\to a$. If an undirected component had an induced cycle of length at least four, take its latest vertex in a topological order of the consistent extension $G$ from step 1.2. Both cycle edges point into that vertex; their other endpoints are nonadjacent, since the cycle has no undirected chord and no directed edge can join vertices in the same component. This is an unshielded collider absent from $P$, contrary to consistency of $G$. Hence every undirected component is chordal.

If $a\to b$ was added by R1 from $d\to a$ with $d,b$ nonadjacent, then either R1 on $d\to a-c$ directly gives $a\to c$, or $d$ is adjacent to $c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-a$ along $c\to d\to a$ gives $c\to a$, and R2 on $c-b$ along $c\to a\to b$ then applies. If $d\to c$, R1 on $d\to c-b$ gives $c\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, the earlier arrow $d\to a$ together with $a-c$ is a counterexample of smaller orientation time, contrary to the choice in step 3.1. Thus this rule case is impossible.

If $a\to b$ was added by R2 from $a\to d\to b$, then $d$ must be adjacent to $c$, since otherwise R1 on $d\to b-c$ orients $b-c$. If $d\to c$, R2 on $a-c$ along $a\to d\to c$ gives $a\to c$. If $c\to d$, R2 on $c-b$ along $c\to d\to b$ gives $c\to b$. If $d-c$ is undirected, the earlier arrow $a\to d$ and $d-c$ form a counterexample of smaller orientation time. All alternatives contradict closure or minimality.

If $a\to b$ was added by R3, there are nonadjacent $d,e$ with $d\to b$, $e\to b$, and undirected $a-d$, $a-e$. Each of $d,e$ is adjacent to $c$, since otherwise R1 on $d\to b-c$ or $e\to b-c$ applies. If $c\to d$ or $c\to e$, R2 on $c-b$ applies along that arrow followed by $d\to b$ or $e\to b$. Otherwise each of $d-c,e-c$ is either undirected or points into $c$. If both point into $c$, R3 on $a-c$ gives $a\to c$. If exactly one points into $c$, say $d\to c$ while $e-c$ is undirected, R1 on $d\to c-e$ gives $c\to e$, and R2 on $c-b$ follows from $c\to e\to b$. If both are undirected, R3 on $c-b$ gives $c\to b$. Every case contradicts the alleged counterexample or closure, proving the claim.

Let $V$ be a finite set of observed vertices, let $G$ be a directed acyclic graph
on $V$, and let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be the endogenous variables of a finite
recursive structural causal model whose observed set is all of $V$ and whose
latent set is empty. The model is Markovian: its exogenous random elements are
mutually independent. Require that the full-joint law $P$ of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$
has a topological probability-kernel factorization: for a topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_p$, its joint law is formed by composing probability kernels
$K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r})$ that depend only on the parents
of $v_r$. Also require that $P$ is faithful to $G$, meaning its conditional
independences among vertex subvectors are exactly the d-separations in $G$.
Assume AC for these probability interfaces.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.

Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

Assume AC, and let a joint law $P$ on the measurable vertex variables of a
finite DAG $G$ be given. The law is **faithful to $G$** if, for every triple
of pairwise disjoint vertex sets $A,B,C$, the conditional independence
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C)$$
implies that $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$. This is the converse of the
global Markov implication; faithfulness is a separate assumption on the
specified law, not a consequence of DAG factorization. No claim about Markov
equivalence, skeletons, or unshielded colliders is included. Here $X_A$ is
the finite random vector $(X_v)_{v\in A}$ with the finite-product
sigma-algebra; for $A=\varnothing$ it is the unique random element of the
empty-product singleton.

Let $G$ be a finite DAG on $V$. For distinct vertices $i,j\in V$, the pair
$\{i,j\}$ is an edge of the skeleton of $G$ if and only if there is no
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ that d-separates $i$ and $j$ in $G$.

Let $i-k-j$ be an unshielded triple in a finite DAG and let
$S\subseteq V\setminus\{i,j\}$ d-separate $i$ and $j$. Then the triple is a
v-structure $i\to k\leftarrow j$ if and only if $k\notin S$.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.

made at level $\ell$.

neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. For each unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, replace $i-k-j$ by
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$.

using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Let $G$ be a finite DAG. Start with its skeleton, orient exactly the edges in
its unshielded colliders, and leave all other edges undirected. Repeatedly apply

class of $G$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F2], every d-separation in $G$ is a conditional independence in its law. By [F3], every conditional independence is a d-separation. Since the oracle is exact by [F1], it answers “independent” exactly for d-separated pairs and sets.

The skeleton search terminates. If $|V|\le1$, it has no pairs to test and stops at level $0$. Otherwise, at each level it processes finitely many pairs and finitely many subsets. An endpoint has at most $|V|-2$ neighbors other than the other endpoint, so at level $\ell=|V|-2$ no remaining edge can meet the condition requiring at least $\ell+1$ such neighbors; the level therefore cannot be incremented past this finite bound. The orientation phase scans finitely many rule instances on the finite vertex set. Every successful application directs one previously undirected edge, which is never undirected again, so there are at most $\binom{|V|}{2}$ successful applications before a scan finds none. Both phases, and hence the algorithm, terminate.

Every true skeleton edge $i-j$ remains in the search graph: its one-edge path is active given every allowed conditioning set, so by [F1] and [F2] no oracle test deletes it. For a nonedge $i-j$, [F4] gives a separating set $S=\operatorname{pa}(i)$ or $\operatorname{pa}(j)$ that excludes the endpoints. Every vertex in that parent set remains adjacent to the chosen endpoint because all true edges remain. At any level $\ell<|S|$ while $i-j$ remains, that endpoint has at least $|S|\ge\ell+1$ other neighbors. The stopping condition therefore cannot stop before level $|S|$, and at that level the algorithm tests $S$ and deletes $i-j$. Thus the returned skeleton is exactly the skeleton of $G$.

Every set recorded when an edge is deleted was accepted by the exact oracle. By step 1.1 it d-separates the deleted endpoints. Since the skeleton from step 2.1 is exact, each unshielded triple is an unshielded triple of $G$; [F5] shows the algorithm orients its middle vertex as a collider exactly when it is a collider in $G$.

The algorithm then applies R1–R3 to closure. Its pattern has the exact skeleton and exactly the unshielded colliders of $G$ by steps 2.1–3.1. Applying [F7] gives the CPDAG of $G$. By step 1.2 the finite procedure terminates, so this is the algorithm's output.

definite, define the residual columns
$$R_{i\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_i,\qquad R_{j\mid S}=(I-\Pi_S)\mathbf x_j.$$
The **sample partial correlation** is
$$\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S}=\frac{R_{i\mid S}^{T}R_{j\mid S}}{\|R_{i\mid S}\|_2\,\|R_{j\mid S}\|_2}.$$
For $-1<r<1$, the **Fisher transform** is
$g(r)=\frac12\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}$, and the sample Fisher statistic is
$Z_{ij\mid S}=g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})$. For a test using multiplier
$\sqrt{n-|S|-3}$, require $n-|S|-3>0$ so that this factor is positive. Under independent samples
from a nondegenerate Gaussian law, the stated covariance block is positive
definite almost surely whenever $n-|S|-3>0$.

invertible; the following theorem proves that $K_{ij\mid S}$ is positive
definite, so this definition applies to every such $i,j,S$.

derivations.claim: Since $q_n=O(n^{1-b})$ with $b>0$, eventually $n-q_n-3>0$, so [F1] makes every sample statistic in the capped search defined almost surely. The sample procedure terminates for every answer sequence: it processes at most $q_n+1$ finite levels, each with finitely many pair-and-subset tests, and its finite R1–R3 closure directs at most $\binom{p_n}{2}$ edges. Since $c_n\le M<1$, take $t=c_n/4\le1$ in [F4]. For every tested triple $(i,j,S)$, the probability that $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})-g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|>c_n/4$ is at most $C_M\exp(-c_M(n-|S|-1)c_n^2/16)$. For large $n$, $q_n/n\to0$ and $n-q_n-1\ge n/2$, so each such probability is at most $C_M\exp(-c'_M n c_n^2)$ for a constant $c'_M>0$.

There are at most $N_n=\binom{p_n}{2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{q_n}\binom{p_n-2}{\ell} \le p_n^2(q_n+1)p_n^{q_n}\le p_n^{q_n+3}$ distinct pair-and-set tests, since $q_n\le p_n-1$ and $q_n+1\le p_n$. A union bound, which requires no independence between tests, shows that the event $E_n$ on which every test of size at most $q_n$ has Fisher-transform error at most $c_n/4$ has failure probability at most $C_M\exp\!\left((q_n+3)\log p_n-c'_M n c_n^2\right).$ The assumptions imply $n c_n^2\ge C_0 n^{1-2d}$ eventually and $(q_n+3)\log p_n=O(n^{1-b}\log n)=o(n^{1-2d})$, because $2d<b$. Thus, after reducing the positive constant in the exponent, $\mathbb P(E_n^c)\le\exp(-C n^{1-2d})$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

On $E_n$, if $\rho_{ij\mid S}=0$, then [F1] gives $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\le c_n/4$. By [F3], this is the population conditional-independence case. Hence $T_{ij\mid S}\le\sqrt n c_n/4<\sqrt n c_n/2$, so the test declares independence. If $\rho_{ij\mid S}\ne0$, then [F2] and the lower-bound hypothesis give $|\rho_{ij\mid S}|\ge c_n$, and $|g(\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge|\rho_{ij\mid S}|$ because $|\operatorname{atanh}(r)|\ge|r|$ for $|r|<1$. Therefore $|g(\widehat\rho_{ij\mid S})|\ge3c_n/4$. Since $(n-|S|-3)/n\ge(n-q_n-3)/n\to1$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $\sqrt{(n-|S|-3)/n}>2/3$, so $T_{ij\mid S}>\sqrt n c_n/2$ and the test declares dependence. By [F3] these are exactly the dependent cases.

On $E_n$ the capped sample PC search makes the same decisions as the uncapped perfect-oracle procedure through level $q_n$. True edges are never removed, because their one-edge paths prevent d-separation and [F7] makes every such test dependent. For each nonedge, [F8] supplies a separating parent set of size at most the true maximum degree $q_n$; its parent edges remain, so the algorithm tests and removes that nonedge no later than level $q_n$. Thus by completion of that level the sample search and the perfect-oracle run have the exact skeleton and the same separating records. The oracle run cannot need another level: on an exact skeleton of maximum degree at most $q_n$, no remaining edge can have an endpoint with the $q_n+1$ other neighbors required to advance after level $q_n$. If either run stops earlier by its ordinary degree condition, their identical decisions make both stop; otherwise both stop after level $q_n$, the sample run by its cap. Their collider and R1–R3 orientations therefore agree, and [F5] identifies the oracle run's output, hence the sample output, as the CPDAG of $G_n$.

The only failure event is contained in $E_n^c$, whose probability has the bound from step 2.1. Step 4.1 identifies the output on $E_n$ as the CPDAG. This proves the stated consistency bound. The threshold uses $c_n$, so the theorem does not provide a data-driven choice of that parameter.

on $V$, and let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be the endogenous variables of a finite
recursive structural causal model whose observed set is all of $V$ and whose
latent set is empty. The model is Markovian: its exogenous random elements are
mutually independent. Require that the full-joint law $P$ of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$
has a topological probability-kernel factorization: for a topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_p$, its joint law is formed by composing probability kernels
$K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r})$ that depend only on the parents
of $v_r$. Also require that $P$ is faithful to $G$, meaning its conditional
independences among vertex subvectors are exactly the d-separations in $G$.
Assume AC for these probability interfaces.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Two finite DAGs on the same vertex set are Markov equivalent, meaning that they
induce the same d-separation relations, if and only if they have the same
skeleton and the same unshielded colliders.

Fix a finite vertex set $V$. For a DAG $G$ on $V$, its **skeleton** is the
undirected graph with edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $G$ contains $i\to j$ or
$j\to i$. An **unshielded triple** is a triple of distinct vertices $i,k,j$
with edges $i-k$ and $k-j$ in the skeleton and no edge between $i$ and $j$.
It is an **unshielded collider** (also called a v-structure) when its arrows are
$i\to k\leftarrow j$. Two DAGs on $V$ are **Markov equivalent** when they
induce the same d-separation relations: for every pairwise disjoint
$A,B,S\subseteq V$, $A$ and $B$ are d-separated by $S$ in one DAG exactly
when they are d-separated by $S$ in the other. The equivalence class of $G$ is
denoted $[G]$.

A **partially directed acyclic graph** (PDAG) on $V$ is a simple mixed graph
whose directed edges contain no directed cycle. A **consistent DAG extension**
of a PDAG preserves every directed edge, orients every undirected edge, is
acyclic, and creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. For an
equivalence class with a common skeleton, its **completed pattern** directs an
edge exactly when that orientation occurs in every DAG of the class and leaves
the edge undirected when both orientations occur. A **completed partially
directed acyclic graph** (CPDAG) for $[G]$ is this unique completed pattern
when its consistent DAG extensions are exactly $[G]$. Thus its directed edges
are compelled, while each undirected edge occurs in both directions among its
consistent extensions.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

**Output:** An undirected skeleton $C$, a separator record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$
for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.
Adjacency sets are read from the current graph, including deletions already
made at level $\ell$.

3. If at least one remaining edge has an endpoint with at least $\ell+1$
neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. For each unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, replace $i-k-j$ by
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$.

5. Repeatedly orient edges to closure under the following background-free rules,
using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Do not apply a background-knowledge rule.

Assume AC and the causally sufficient perfect-oracle discovery regime for a
finite observed DAG $G$ and its full-joint law. The population PC algorithm
with any fixed vertex order terminates and returns exactly the skeleton of $G$,
records a d-separating set for every deleted pair, orients exactly the
unshielded colliders of $G$, and returns the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m$ be a finite independent family of scalar normal variables with means $\mu_r$ and variances $\sigma_r^2$. For real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m,b$, [F3] gives the characteristic function of $b+\sum_r a_rW_r$ as $\exp\!\left(it(b+\sum_r a_r\mu_r)-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_r a_r^2\sigma_r^2\right)$; scalar uniqueness identifies this as the normal law with that mean and variance. Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F4] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero.

In the latent model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, by independence of $L,U_X,U_Y$. In the direct-edge model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac32=2$. Both vectors are Gaussian by step 1.1 and have the same positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$. By [F5], both vector characteristic functions equal $\exp(-t^T\Sigma t/2)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R^2$; the uniqueness clause of [F5] gives equality of the full observed laws.

The latent model is a finite recursive Markovian SCM with observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and omitted latent vertex $L$, so it does not satisfy [F2]. The direct-edge model has observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and independent exogenous variables; its full-joint law factors as $N(0,2)(dx)N(x/2,3/2)(dy)$, the root probability kernel for $X$ followed by the probability kernel for $Y$ given its parent $X$. In its two-vertex graph $X\to Y$, the only pair of nonempty disjoint endpoint sets is $\{X\},\{Y\}$, which is not d-separated because of the direct path; step 1.2 gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, so they are not independent. Thus this law is faithful to the direct-edge DAG, and the direct-edge model satisfies the observed-only Markovian factorization and faithfulness conditions in the discovery regime. Since the observed laws agree by step 1.2, no procedure using only that law can distinguish the two causal explanations.

The common observed law has $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1\ne0$, so $X,Y$ are dependent and the perfect oracle does not delete their only edge. With only two vertices there is no unshielded triple and none of R1–R3 applies; by [F9] the regime-compliant run terminates, and its computed output is $X-Y$. Reversing the single edge in the direct-edge DAG keeps the same skeleton and no unshielded collider, so [F6] proves the reverse DAG is equivalent; [F7] therefore gives the same undirected CPDAG. The PC output reports adjacency but cannot recover the latent-versus-direct causal distinction.
